entries.clause: Anyone in crisis who needs help at once is told to ring triple zero (000). [...] Suicide Call Back Service, on 1300 659 467: support for a person who feels suicidal, or for someone worried about them, 24/7. [...] Beyond Blue, on 1300 22 4636: help for a person or someone they love, by phone 24 hours a day, every day, or by online chat. [...] MensLine Australia, on 1300 78 99 78: counselling for men in Australia by phone or online, 24 hours a day, every day. [...] Kids Helpline, on 1800 55 1800: free, private counselling, 24/7, for those aged 5 to 25 (children and young people). [...] 13YARN, on 13 92 76: crisis support at no cost, kept confidential, 24/7. [...] Brother to Brother, on 1800 435 799: a crisis line open 24/7 for Aboriginal men facing family violence. [...] Open Arms, on 1800 011 046: counselling at no cost, kept confidential, 24/7, for anyone with at least one day's service in the Australian Defence Force. [...] 1800RESPECT, on 1800 737 732: support, 24/7, for those facing domestic or family violence. [...] Translating and Interpreting Service, on 131 450: help, 24/7, to reach a mental health helpline in one's own language. [...] National Relay Service, on 0423 677 767: free, confidential relay help, 24/7, for a call to a mental health helpline. [...] healthdirect helpline, on 1800 022 222 (in Victoria, NURSE-ON-CALL): a registered nurse to talk to, 24 hours a day, every day.

entries.issuing_body: World Health Organization and the International Association for Suicide Prevention
entries.title: Preventing suicide: a resource for media professionals, update 2023
entries.jurisdiction: None: international guidance, applied here to a one-to-one reply rather than to media
entries.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO, as the document states ("This work is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 IGO licence"). G6 quotes short clauses only, with this citation, and suggests no endorsement by WHO.
entries.clause: stories of overcoming a suicidal crisis can lead to fewer suicides [...] Don’t describe the method used. [...] Don’t use language/content which sensationalizes, romanticizes or normalizes suicide, or that presents it as a viable solution to problems. [...] Do provide accurate information about where and how to seek help for suicidal thoughts and suicidal crises. [...] Information about support services should be provided at the end of the news story or, even better, at the beginning of all stories about suicide. [...] Only a limited number of services should be mentioned [...] The contact details of listed services should be checked regularly to ensure that they are accurate. [...] to include the message that people who are suicidal should seek help, to indicate how they can access that help [...] It is also helpful to report stories about how some people have reached out to support others in crisis
entries.section: Page xiii (Papageno: overcoming a crisis); the quick reference guide, pages xiv and xv (the Dos and Don'ts); pages 11 and 12 (where to seek help, how many services, the help-seeking message, reaching out to others)

entries.clause: Some wording can do harm when suicide is discussed. [...] Terms that make suicide sound like an outcome to want, such as 'successful suicide' and 'unsuccessful suicide' [...] Terms that tie suicide to crime or sin, such as 'committed suicide' and 'commit suicide' [...] A term that sensationalises suicide, such as 'suicide epidemic' [...] Terms that glamourise an attempt, such as 'failed suicide' and 'suicide bid' [...] Uses of the word 'suicide' where no suicide is meant, such as 'political suicide' and 'suicide mission'
